title: THE FATHER WHOSE FAMILY SECRETS WERE WRITTEN INTO THE BIBLE—AND THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO ERASE THEIR NAMES
paragraphs: THE FATHER WHOSE FAMILY SECRETS WERE WRITTEN INTO THE BIBLE—AND THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO ERASE THEIR NAMES
Two wives. A concubine. Children born into a complicated family. And a genealogy that reveals something extraordinary: God does not need a spotless family history to accomplish His purposes.
“And Caleb the son of Hezron begat children of Azubah his wife, and of Jerioth: her sons are these; Jesher, and Shobab, and Ardon.” — 1 Chronicles 2:18, KJV
Imagine opening the Bible and discovering that God had preserved your family's history.
Not the carefully edited version.
Not the beautiful family portrait where everyone smiles, everyone looks happy, and nobody mentions what happened behind closed doors.
The real history.
The marriages. The children. The losses. The relationships that are difficult to explain. The names people remember. The names people wish everyone would forget.
Now imagine that history remaining in Scripture for thousands of years.
That is what makes 1 Chronicles 2:18–24 so remarkable.

At first glance, it looks like another ancient genealogy. Names. Marriages. Children. Generations. The kind of passage many readers quietly skip because they are searching for something more inspiring.
But slow down.
Because buried in these verses is a family history that refuses to fit neatly into a picture of domestic perfection.
And somewhere inside that uncomfortable reality is a question that may reach into your own life.
What happens when the story you inherited is not the story you would have chosen?
What happens when your family history includes things you cannot change?
What happens when the people who came before you made decisions that still affect you?
And what happens when you begin to wonder whether the brokenness behind you has already determined the future ahead of you?
Before we answer, we need to meet the family Scripture actually describes.
Because the truth is more interesting—and more challenging—than a sentimental retelling.
The passage begins with Caleb, the son of Hezron.
This is not the famous Caleb who accompanied Joshua into Canaan and later declared his confidence in God's promise. This Caleb belongs to a different genealogical setting within the tribe of Judah.
The distinction matters.
When we read Scripture carefully, we honor the people and events God has actually placed before us rather than borrowing details from another biblical story.
In 1 Chronicles 2:18, Caleb is associated with Azubah, identified as his wife, and with Jerioth. The text then names Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.
The Hebrew wording is compact and somewhat difficult.

It identifies Azubah as a wife but does not explain Jerioth's relationship to Caleb with the same clarity. Some interpreters understand Jerioth as another wife; others suggest that Jerioth may be another name for Azubah or understand the family relationship differently.
Scripture does not settle that question explicitly.
That means we should not confidently announce that Caleb had two wives on the basis of this verse alone.
The passage does, however, plainly describe multiple family relationships, a later marriage, and a concubine within this extended genealogy.
And it does something else.
It remembers the women.
Azubah.
Jerioth.
Ephrath.
Maachah.
Women whose lives cannot be reconstructed completely from the few words preserved about them.
We are not told what they feared.
We are not told how they felt.
We are not told whether their homes were peaceful or painful.
And we must resist the temptation to invent their emotions as though Scripture had revealed them.
But their names remain.
Think about that.
Centuries passed. Kingdoms rose and fell. Cities were destroyed. Generations disappeared into history.
Yet these names survived in the biblical record.
Not because we know every detail of their lives.
But because they belonged to a history the chronicler considered important to preserve.
Then the story changes.
“And when Azubah was dead, Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur.” — 1 Chronicles 2:19, KJV
There it is.
A death.
One sentence.
No funeral description. No recorded farewell. No account of the days that followed.
Azubah died.
And Caleb married Ephrath.
It is possible to read those words in seconds.
But anyone who has buried someone they love knows that the space between those two events could contain an ocean of grief.
The Bible does not tell us how Caleb mourned, so we cannot claim to know.
Still, the brevity of the record reminds us of something deeply human.
Sometimes the greatest turning points in a person's life are compressed into a single sentence.
“My mother died.”
“My father left.”
“Our marriage ended.”
“We lost the baby.”
“Everything changed that year.”
A sentence can be short while the suffering behind it lasts for years.
Maybe that is why this genealogy deserves more than a hurried glance.
It reminds us that biblical names belonged to real people, not merely to religious vocabulary.
They lived in a world where death interrupted households, marriages reshaped families, and children were born into circumstances they had not chosen.
Just like us.
But the passage continues.
Ephrath gives birth to Hur.
Hur becomes the father of Uri.
Uri becomes the father of Bezaleel, also called Bezalel.
And suddenly, a name from this genealogy connects with one of the most beautiful assignments in Israel's wilderness history.
In Exodus 31:1–5, the Lord identifies Bezalel, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah.
God fills him with His Spirit, giving him wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and skill for artistic craftsmanship.
His assignment?
To help create the sacred furnishings of the tabernacle.
The place associated with God's dwelling among His covenant people.
Do you see the connection?
A genealogy that records family death and remarriage leads to a man whom God equips for holy craftsmanship.
Not because his ancestors were flawless.
Not because every relationship in his family history was an example to imitate.
But because God's purposes were not limited by the imperfections of earlier generations.
That is not permission to romanticize complicated relationships.
It is a reason to marvel at divine grace.
God's ability to work through a family does not mean God approves of everything that family has done.
We need that distinction.
Because without it, we can turn biblical description into biblical permission.
And Scripture does not allow us to do that.
The Bible records polygamy, concubinage, betrayal, violence, jealousy, and devastating family conflict.
Recording something is not the same as commanding it.
Preserving a person's name is not the same as approving every decision that person made.
God's design for marriage is rooted in Genesis 2:24, where a man and his wife become one flesh. Jesus returns to that foundation in Matthew 19:4–6, emphasizing the covenant union God established.
So when we encounter complicated household arrangements in ancient genealogies, we should not pretend that every arrangement represents God's ideal.
But neither should we miss the astonishing reality that God continued working through imperfect human histories.
And that brings us to another part of the passage.
In 1 Chronicles 2:21, Hezron marries the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead, when Hezron is sixty years old. She bears him Segub, who becomes the father of Jair.
Then, in verse 24, after Hezron's death, Abiah bears Ashur, identified as the father of Tekoa.
Even the chronology and wording of verse 24 have generated interpretive discussion, especially concerning its geographical language in the Hebrew text.
These are not verses that give us every detail we might want.
They are fragments of a much larger history.
And the surrounding genealogy becomes even more striking when we continue just beyond the assigned passage.
“And Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bare Haran, and Moza, and Gazez.” — 1 Chronicles 2:46, KJV
There is the explicit reference to a concubine.
Her name was Ephah.

A concubine in the ancient biblical world was a woman in a recognized but generally lower-status household relationship than a primary wife. Such arrangements were embedded in the social structures of the time, often involving unequal standing and power.
The text does not give us enough information to reconstruct Ephah's personal circumstances or emotional experience.
But it names her.
And it names her children.
Haran.
Moza.
Gazez.
It would be easy to rush past those names.
But pause for a moment.
Because every child named in a genealogy was once a child entering a world already shaped by adults.
No child chooses the circumstances of conception.
No child chooses the status assigned to a mother.
No child chooses whether a household is peaceful, divided, wealthy, poor, respected, or disgraced.
And no child should be made to carry moral blame for circumstances they did not create.
Perhaps you understand that more deeply than most.
Perhaps you grew up answering questions you never wanted anyone to ask.
Perhaps people whispered about your parents.
Perhaps your family history included infidelity, abandonment, addiction, abuse, or a relationship that the community treated as scandalous.
Perhaps you learned early that some people judge children by the decisions of their parents.
And perhaps, without realizing it, you began to believe them.
You started wondering whether your beginning made you less worthy of love.
Whether your family name made you less welcome.
Whether your past had already placed a ceiling over your future.
If that is you, there is something you need to hear.
You are responsible for your own response to God, but you are not guilty simply because of the sins committed by those who came before you.
Ezekiel 18:20 teaches that a son does not bear the guilt of his father merely because he is his son.
That does not mean families never experience the consequences of earlier decisions.
They often do.
Sin can wound people across generations.
A father's cruelty can shape a child's fears.
A mother's abandonment can leave questions that last decades.
A broken household can affect the way someone understands trust, love, and safety.
Consequences are real.
But inherited circumstances are not the same as inherited personal guilt.
And your family's history is not the final authority over your identity.
God is.
Yet we must go deeper.
Because Christianity is not simply a message that says, “Your past does not define you.”
That can be comforting, but by itself it is incomplete.
The Gospel tells us something more searching.
Even if we came from the most respectable family imaginable, we would still need a Savior.
Even if nobody had ever whispered about our parents, we would still need forgiveness.
Even if our family tree contained generations of admirable people, their goodness could not make us righteous before God.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
The person raised in a broken home.
And the person raised in a loving one.
The child of scandal.
And the child of privilege.
The one carrying wounds caused by others.
And the one who has caused wounds through personal sin.
We do not all carry the same experiences or responsibilities.
But every one of us needs the grace of Jesus Christ.
And that is where this ancient genealogy begins to point us toward something far greater than itself.
Because the Bible does not end with Caleb's family.
It moves through generations toward the fulfillment of God's promises in Jesus.
Matthew opens his Gospel with another genealogy.
And it is astonishingly honest.
Judah and Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
David and the wife of Uriah.
Names and descriptions that call attention to complicated histories, outsider status, human wrongdoing, suffering, and the surprising ways God's redemptive purposes unfold.
Consider how Matthew 1:6 identifies Solomon's mother.
It does not simply present a polished royal family portrait.
It remembers her through the description “her that had been the wife of Urias” in the King James Version.
The reference draws our attention back to David's grievous sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah in 2 Samuel 11.
David abused his royal power, committed adultery, and arranged Uriah's death.
Scripture does not excuse him.
God confronted him through Nathan.
David's repentance did not erase every consequence of what he had done.
Yet God's covenant purposes continued, and the genealogy of Jesus includes this history.
That is grace without denial.
Mercy without pretending evil was harmless.
Redemption without rewriting sin as righteousness.
And here is where the message becomes personal.
Some people think grace means God looks at their lives and says, “Nothing was wrong.”
But biblical grace is far more powerful.
Grace does not require God to deny the truth.
Grace means God can forgive sinners because Jesus Christ has dealt with sin through His death and resurrection.
The Greek word commonly translated “grace” in the New Testament is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor and gift, and in passages such as Ephesians 2:8–9 it directs us toward salvation received from God rather than earned through our works.
Read the words carefully:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
A gift.
Not a reward for having the right family.
Not a prize for maintaining a spotless reputation.
Not a payment for religious performance.
Not something purchased through financial generosity.
A gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the word translated “redeemed” in passages such as Ephesians 1:7 comes from the Greek ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis), conveying release or deliverance through redemption.
Ephesians 1:7 declares:
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.”
Not redemption through ancestry.
Not redemption through public approval.
Not redemption through pretending the past never happened.
Redemption through His blood.
This is why the cross must remain at the center of everything we say about broken families, restoration, forgiveness, and hope.
Because without the cross, we might reduce Christianity to encouragement.
And encouragement, however sincere, cannot atone for sin.
Only Jesus saves.
Imagine standing before God with every chapter of your life opened.
The things you inherited.
The things you suffered.
The things you chose.
The things you concealed.
The moments you were wronged.
And the moments you were the one who did wrong.
Nothing hidden.
Nothing edited.
Nothing softened for appearances.
What could possibly give a sinner hope before a holy God?
Not a perfect explanation.
Not a respectable surname.
Not a collection of good deeds.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God, crucified and risen.
He did not come merely to make our stories sound more beautiful.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or heart that, in biblical context, involves turning away from sin toward God.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is not being sorry only because consequences arrived.
It is bringing our sin into the light, acknowledging God's truth, and turning to Him in faith.
That may mean confessing dishonesty.
Ending a sinful relationship.
Seeking forgiveness from someone we harmed.
Making restitution where possible.
Abandoning secret habits that have been destroying our integrity.
Or finally admitting that our religious appearance has been covering a heart far from God.
And if you are the one who was wounded by another person's sin, repentance does not mean accepting blame for what was done to you.
You do not have to call abuse love.
You do not have to pretend betrayal was harmless.
You do not have to return to danger to prove that you have forgiven.
Christ's truth makes room for both mercy and justice.
That is why His grace is not shallow.
It reaches deeper than our carefully managed appearances.
And sometimes the most difficult person to bring into the light is not the person everybody knows is struggling.
It is the person everybody thinks is doing fine.
The father who provides for his children but cannot remember the last time he prayed with them.
The mother who encourages everyone else while privately feeling spiritually exhausted.
The church member who knows the right words but has stopped speaking honestly to God.
The believer who posts Bible verses but avoids the conversation that could begin genuine reconciliation.
The person who has built an entire identity around never letting anyone know how badly they need help.
You may have spent years protecting the image of your life.
But Jesus did not die to preserve your image.
He died to save you.
And perhaps that is the sentence you have been avoiding.
Not because you disagree with it.
But because accepting it means surrendering the illusion that you can heal yourself through secrecy, achievement, or religious performance.
The Gospel does not invite you to become better at hiding.
It invites you to come to Christ.
And that is why the genealogies matter.
They remind us that Scripture is not a collection of imaginary perfect people.
It is the record of God's dealings with real humanity.
People who lived.
People who died.
People who married.
People who sinned.
People who suffered.
People whose names were remembered long after the world forgot their voices.
Yet we should be careful not to make the genealogy say more than it says.
First Chronicles 2:18–24 does not tell us that Caleb repented of a particular sin.
It does not describe Azubah's private grief.
It does not reveal Jerioth's feelings.
It does not tell us that every member of the family experienced spiritual transformation.
And it does not teach that complicated relationships are automatically blessed because they appear in the biblical record.
What it does show is that these lives and family connections were preserved within the history of Judah.
When read alongside the wider testimony of Scripture, that history reminds us that God's saving purposes unfold in a world marked by human frailty, suffering, and sin.
The fullest revelation of His grace is not found in our speculation about ancient families.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
And now, perhaps, the question is no longer about Caleb.
Perhaps the question is about you.
What have you allowed your family history to tell you about your worth?
What secret have you mistaken for your permanent identity?
What failure have you treated as though it were stronger than the blood of Christ?
What relationship have you refused to bring before God because you fear what obedience might require?
And what would happen if, instead of trying to rewrite the past yourself, you surrendered your future to the One who makes all things new?
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise is not a guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears the moment someone believes.
Scars may remain.
Grief may continue.
Trust may require time to rebuild.
Some relationships may never be restored in this life.
But union with Christ means that the believer's standing before God and direction of life have been fundamentally changed.
The past is no longer the final verdict.
Sin is no longer the rightful master.
Condemnation is no longer the destiny of those who belong to Christ.
And that is a hope worth holding onto when your emotions have not yet caught up with what God has promised.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting alone.
Maybe your marriage is struggling.
Maybe you are a father who knows he has failed his children and wants to begin making things right.
Maybe you are a mother who has spent years carrying shame that was never hers to carry.
Maybe you are a son or daughter still trying to understand why the adults in your childhood made the choices they did.
Maybe you have been attending church for years, but you know there is a part of your life you have never truly surrendered to Jesus.
This is not an invitation to pretend your pain is small.
It is an invitation to bring your whole life to a Savior who is greater than your pain and your sin.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ, do not confuse knowing Christian language with knowing Him.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Believe that He died for sinners and rose again.
Receive His mercy by faith.
And begin following Him—not because your life is already perfect, but because He is Lord.
If you have wandered from Him, return.
If you have sinned against someone, take responsibility.
If you need help, seek it.
If you are wounded, do not be ashamed to ask for prayer and wise support.
If you are exhausted, remember that Christ's invitation is not reserved for people who have everything together.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
That invitation still stands.
Not for the sake of appearances.
Not because you owe strangers an explanation of your pain.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response becomes the beginning of a meaningful conversation.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus has helped you turn away from sin, endure suffering, or begin rebuilding what was broken, consider sharing it.
Your testimony will not replace the Gospel.
But it may help another person recognize that they are not alone in needing the Savior.
Think about someone you know.
Someone who feels ashamed of their family.
Someone who believes their mistakes have disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has stopped opening the Bible because they feel unworthy.
Someone who smiles in public while quietly wondering whether God could still welcome them.
Because one article may encourage someone for a day.
But a life rooted in God's Word needs nourishment again and again.
That is why Gospel Warrior continues developing resources for people who want more than passing inspiration.
And if this ministry has helped strengthen your faith, there is another meaningful way you can participate.
Not because a payment earns God's favor.
Not because salvation, grace, or spiritual maturity can be purchased.
They cannot.
But because supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a genuine expression of Christian generosity and partnership.
Philippians 1:5 speaks of partnership in the Gospel, and Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers materially supported Paul's ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 also reminds us that giving should be willing and cheerful, not compelled.
But voluntary, faithful support can help make more teaching, more discipleship resources, and more Gospel-centered content possible.
Think about the difference between reading something that encourages you and helping make that same encouragement available to someone else.
A believer struggling with temptation.
A parent looking for biblical guidance.
A young person trying to understand the Gospel.
We cannot promise how many people will respond.
Only God knows the full fruit of any ministry.
But we can faithfully sow the Word and trust Him with the outcome.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of Scripture and opportunities to encourage others, but they are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
The Gospel is.
The mission is to make Jesus known, help believers grow in His Word, and continue pointing people toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformation.
Christ has already paid the price of our redemption.
Our response is gratitude, worship, obedience, and love.
That brings us back to where we began.
An ancient father.
A genealogy.
Women whose names survived the centuries.
Children whose family circumstances were recorded without the explanations modern readers might want.
Death.
Remarriage.
A concubine in the wider family record.
And a descendant named Bezalel, whom God equipped for sacred work.
It would be easy to leave this passage thinking only about the complications of an ancient household.
But perhaps the greater lesson is that the Bible invites us to look at human history without pretending that human beings are flawless.
And then it directs our attention to the only One who truly is.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who entered real human history.
The Holy One who never sinned.
The Lamb of God who bore the sins of His people.
The risen Lord who offers forgiveness and new life.
Your story may contain chapters you would never have chosen.
Some may have been written through the sins of others.
Some may be chapters for which you must personally repent.
Some may still bring tears when you remember them.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, none of those chapters has greater authority than His finished work.
You do not have to deny the past.
You do not have to glorify the scandal.
You do not have to call evil good.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent where repentance is needed.
You can seek healing where wounds remain.
You can forgive without pretending that justice does not matter.
And you can trust the Savior who is able to bring redemption into the most complicated human stories.
Because the greatest miracle is not that God can make an embarrassing family history sound respectable.
It is that God can take guilty sinners, forgive them through Jesus Christ, and make them His own.
And when the world tries to tell you that your beginning has already decided your ending, remember the cross.
The pages behind you may still carry the scars, but in Christ, the final word belongs to grace.
